extracted.intended_audience: comic artists, illustrators, and graphic designers creating sequential art/page layouts
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for constructing a reusable page grid for comics (using a 1.5 ratio/system-of-thirds) and using gutters, staggered panels, and circular/linear composition guides to control reading flow and page harmony.

rubrics_metrics.name: System of 3rds
rubrics_metrics.description: This grid is equally divided into 3rds across the vertical axis by overlapping two squares so that the top square terminates at the middle of the bottom square — making the inverse true of the bottom square.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use overlapping squares to create three equal horizontal guides; this gives a consistent structural rhythm for laying out panels across the page. The author deliberately uses a 1.5 ratio (rather than the classical golden ratio) because it is common in comics. Apply this system as the underlying scaffold before placing panels and composition guides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel Gutters
rubrics_metrics.description: After I draw the squares, I align my horizontal gutters on the axis where the squares overlap. I also add an extra gutter notation in the middle in case I ever want to do a half-page panel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place horizontal gutters along the overlap axes of the 3rds grid. Include a middle gutter guide to allow flexible layouts (e.g., half-page panels). A gutter is defined as 'the space that separates panels in a comic.' Aligning gutters to the grid ensures predictable reading flow and panel sizing options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiated Gutter Sizes
rubrics_metrics.description: Next, I divide the horizontal area in half two times — creating four potential panels across. I keep the vertical gutters thinner than the horizontal gutters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make vertical gutters thinner than horizontal ones so that greater horizontal proximity encourages the reader to group each row of panels for easier reading. This differentiation helps visually separate rows while keeping panels in the same row read together. Avoid equal-width gutters that make row grouping ambiguous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Panel Staggering
rubrics_metrics.description: I noticed that [Hergé] staggered the gutters of his comics. I came to the realization that this was to prevent what designers called 'rivers.' A river occurs when there is a gap in information that coincides with a gap below. The danger is that a reader might drop down to the next line of info before completing the first one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place gutters to the left and right of the middle gutter guide so panels can be staggered across rows. Staggering prevents vertical 'rivers' of empty space that can interrupt the intended left-to-right/top-to-bottom reading order. Avoid stacking perfectly aligned vertical gaps that form continuous columns of negative space.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Excessive Thin Panels (limit four-across)
rubrics_metrics.description: I rarely use four panels horizontally across a page because they are so thin, but I will often use two panels per row.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be cautious about creating too many narrow panels across a page — panels that are too slim reduce visual clarity and storytelling space. Favor two panels per row or otherwise ensure panel widths are adequate for content. If you must use multiple columns, ensure panel content remains legible and compositionally strong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Circular and Linear Composition Guides
rubrics_metrics.description: After creating three horizontal guides, I place circles in the squares that result. Additionally, I include guides at 45 degrees that connect with the corners of each square and the center of the gutters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use circle overlays and diagonal (45°) guides to help arrange focal points and alignments within panels and across the page. These guides aid in creating harmony (aligning important elements along the guides) or intentional dissonance (placing elements off-guide). They help organize compositions in parallel and perpendicular axes for consistent visual flow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use the Grid to Create Harmony Across Multiple Pages
rubrics_metrics.description: How I use these visual systems to create harmonious compositions across multiple pages of a comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the same grid system across consecutive pages to maintain compositional continuity and visual rhythm through a sequence. Repeating alignments and guide-based focal placements helps the book feel cohesive; alter guides intentionally when you want to break rhythm for dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directing Reader Flow with Visual Elements
rubrics_metrics.description: When using the grid, I try to make sure that at the end of each row, there is a visual element that directs the reader to the bottom left of the page. This might be the direction that a character is facing, or an object that a character is using to point with such as: an algae kabob, dagger, beak, fin, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place characters, gestures, or objects that point or face toward the entry point of the next row (typically bottom-left) to guide eye movement. Conversely, consistently facing characters in opposite directions can create visual dissonance and emphasize tension. Use these cues intentionally to control pacing and reading order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition Inside Panels (use of diagonals)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is important to recognize that composition within panels helps the reading flow just as much as the gutters and layout of the overall page. I also focus especially on the use of diagonals. They are an easy way to make the comic dynamic during points in the story that can come across as bland without them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design internal panel compositions with dynamic lines (diagonals) to increase energy and guide the eye. Use internal composition to support the page-level reading path; avoid flat, static compositions when the narrative calls for motion or emphasis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grid Construction Specifics (page size, ratio, content area)
rubrics_metrics.description: Santoro’s articles encouraged me to develop my own blue-line grid using similar notations, but not by utilizing the Golden Ratio of 1.61803398875. This system uses a 1.5 ratio which is quite common in the comic world. The page dimensions are 11” x 17”. My inside content area is 10” X 15”.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build your template around concrete page and content-area dimensions and a chosen ratio (here 1.5). Know your trim/bleed/safe areas when creating the grid so artwork and gutters stay within printable/safe regions. Use consistent units so the grid can be applied and reproduced reliably.

rubrics_metrics.name: Workflow: physical drafting to digital finishing
rubrics_metrics.description: My personal preference is to use a light box to physically draw the grid in pencil on a piece of bristol paper. I then draw my panels and images (also using pencil) based on completed thumbnail sketches. I then ink them directly on the paper and color it digitally on a computer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a light box and blue-line grid on bristol for tactile control during pencils and inks; scan or photograph for digital coloring. Start from thumbnails, transfer layouts to board with the grid, ink on board, then complete colors digitally. This preserves the handcrafted line while enabling digital finishing.
